deep.reconstruction:
WHAT IS TABULATED (my identification, verified numerically). Let rho = 648000/pi = 206264.806 (arc-seconds per radian). Each tabulated angle v (degrees, minutes, seconds to 1e-5 arc-second) satisfies

  N'' = rho*(2*tan(v/2) + (2/3)*tan(v/2)^3),  equivalently  tan(v/2) + tan(v/2)^3/3 = N''/(2*rho).

This is Barker's equation of parabolic motion, solved for the true anomaly v given the 'mean-anomaly-like' argument N expressed in arc-seconds. Gauss writes it in Theoria Motus, art. 19, as tan(v/2) + (1/3)tan^3(v/2) = k*t/(sqrt(2)*q^(3/2)). The page is part of an inverse Barker table, continued on p.188.

The page has two parts.

(A) Left half. The argument is 300, 302, ..., 424, in units of 100 arc-seconds, so N = 30000'' ... 42400''.
- Column 2 is v.
- Column 3 is the first difference Delta = v(n+2) - v(n), written as the seconds part of 3'17.89475'' etc., with the leading 3' suppressed. For example, 21'32.84598 - 18'14.95123 = 3'17.89475.
- Column 4 is the (negative) second difference in units of 1e-5''. For example, 197.89475 - 197.86700 = 0.02775.
- The entry 2757 against row 300 belongs to the preceding interval 298-300.

(B) Right half, headed 'Log:'. The argument is log10 N = 4.582, 4.584, ..., 4.750 (step 0.002).
- Column 2 is v; it runs from 10 deg 32'58.55'' to 15 deg 25'53.86''.
- Column 3 is the first difference in seconds. For example, 35'51.87150 - 32'58.55490 = 173.31660. Its placement alternates between lower and upper rows.
- Column 4 is the (positive) second difference. For example, 174.08940 - 173.31660 = 0.77280.

The two halves are mutually consistent. Linear interpolation of part B at log10(40000) = 4.60206 gives 11 deg 2'26.88'' + 0.03*181.2'' ≈ 11 deg 2'32.3''. This agrees with part A's 11 deg 2'32.30572'' at N = 40000.

HOW I FOUND IT. The deficits N - v are 105.049'', 247.694'' and 680.273'' at N = 30000'', 40000'' and 56234.13''. They fit v = x - x^3/6 + c x^5 + ... with x = N/rho, and inversion gives x = v + v^3/6 + 7v^5/240 + ...

This is exactly the expansion of 2T + (2/3)T^3 with T = tan(v/2). Indeed 2T = v + v^3/12 + v^5/120 and (2/3)T^3 = v^3/12 + v^5/48.

Direct checks:
- v = 8 deg 18'14.95123'' gives 2T + 2T^3/3 = 0.14544411; compare 30000/rho = 0.14544410.
- v = 11 deg 2'32.30572'' gives 0.19392550; compare 0.19392547.
- v = 15 deg 25'53.85918'' gives 0.27263080; compare 10^4.75/rho = 0.2726306.

The differences of all orders are carried for interpolation; the second differences in particular serve as a smoothness check. The purpose is a working table for computing parabolic (comet) orbits, entering either with the argument itself or with its logarithm.

results.what: Table of true anomaly v versus argument N (arc-seconds, step 200'') and versus log10 N (step 0.002), defined by tan(v/2)+tan^3(v/2)/3 = N/(2 rho), with first and second differences
results.modern_name: Inverse Barker table / solution of Barker's equation for parabolic orbits
results.usually_credited_to: Barker's table (Thomas Barker, 1757); the equation goes back to Halley/Euler/Lambert; parabolic tables were standard in 18th-19th c. astronomy (Olbers 1797, Gauss Theoria Motus 1809)

results.what: Use of systematic first and second differences to check and interpolate a computed table

deep.surprise_reason: A carefully computed inverse Barker (parabolic-motion) table with difference columns is routine computational astronomy, and Gauss's work on parabolic orbits and their tables is well documented (Theoria Motus 1809, art. 19 and related tables). The only mild interest is the high precision (1e-5 arc-second) and the log-argument format.
